verses.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.
Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.”
God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

Yahweh God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all livestock, and above every animal of the field. You shall go on your belly and you shall eat dust all the days of your life.
I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. In pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life.
It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.
By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.
Yahweh God made coats of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
Yahweh God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...”
Therefore Yahweh God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken.
So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim  at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.

footnotes.content: The serpent's first move is not a denial but a question, and a crooked one — 'any tree?' God had opened the whole garden and withheld one. I have watched how much damage a slightly wrong question can do in a heart that is already listening. Notice, too, that he comes to the woman with God's own words in his mouth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She answers well at first, beginning with what is allowed: 'We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden.' There is quiet wisdom in that order. When I am tempted, the battle usually turns on whether I keep God's generosity in front of me before I look at the one thing He has kept back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She adds a fence God never built — 'You shall not touch it.' Fear had already begun editing the command, making it stricter than it was. I have done this myself, guarding against a sin by shrinking the good things around it. God said, do not eat; her memory had already made Him sound harsher than He is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the first flat contradiction of God's word: 'You won't surely die.' Not a question now, but a denial, spoken to a woman who had only ever known God as the giver of every tree. I have heard that same voice in my own thoughts, always reasonable, always assuring me that the warning was an exaggeration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lie is wrapped around a half-truth. Their eyes would indeed open — but not into godhood. They were already made in God's image; the serpent sold them what they already had. That is the shape of every temptation I know: something real is offered, and the gift already given is quietly despised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three things pull at her at once: good for food, a delight to the eyes, desirable to make one wise. The apostle John would later name that same trio — the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, the pride of life (1 John 2:16). She took, she ate, and then she gave to her husband, who was standing there with her. The verse is painfully calm about it all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their eyes were opened, just as promised, and the first thing they saw was their own nakedness. They sewed fig leaves together — the first handmade religion, and it was already too small. I have worn a few fig leaves myself, and they never survive the afternoon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They heard Him walking in the garden in the cool of the day, the hour they had surely loved before, and they hid. Among the trees He had made for them, from the One who made them. Sin's first instinct is not defiance but concealment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God calls, 'Where are you?' — not because He has lost track, but because He wants the man to speak. Readers today hear an echo of that in every honest prayer: the Father still asks the question first, still walking toward the sound of footsteps rather than waiting to be found. As of 2026-10, I am grateful that the seeking has always begun on His side.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid.' Fear enters the story here for the first time, and it comes wearing shame. Before this there was nothing in the garden to be afraid of — least of all God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God does not shout; He asks. 'Who told you that you were naked?' Then the plain question about the tree. He is giving the man room to say it himself, which is what a good father does when he already knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man answers by handing the blame down the line — the woman, and then God for giving her to him: 'the woman whom you gave to be with me.' I have heard this grammar in my own mouth, arranging the story so that I am only ever the recipient of someone else's fault.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God turns to the woman with a shorter, gentler question: 'What have you done?' Her answer is true but not whole — the serpent did deceive her, and she did eat. Both halves belong together. Half the truth is how we usually confess.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the only sentence in the chapter that begins with a curse, and it makes the serpent the lowest thing in the field: on his belly, eating dust. The creature that spoke as though it stood above God's word is put under everyone's feet. There is a kind of justice in that which I find steadying.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the story turns: hostility is placed between the serpent and the woman, between his offspring and hers. One will bruise the head, the other only the heel — the wound is real on both sides, but only one is fatal. The church has long heard in this verse the first whisper of the gospel, and I read it now with the cross in view, where the heel was bruised and the head was crushed (Romans 16:20).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To the woman He speaks of the two places her life would most ache: bearing children, and belonging to her husband. The very gifts meant to be her joy now carry pain and struggle inside them. He does not explain it away; He names it — and then He keeps speaking, which is itself a mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice that He says 'because you listened to your wife's voice' — not because she spoke, but because he listened to her instead of to God. And then a strange tenderness: 'the ground is cursed for your sake.' Even the hardship is aimed at his good, though it would take him a lifetime to see it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thorns and thistles — the ground begins to push back, and every gardener since has known this verse in their hands. The Gospels tell us soldiers twisted thorns into a crown and set it on Jesus' head. I have never read that line without thinking of this one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.' It is less a cruel sentence than a true one, and the psalms take comfort in it: God remembers our frame, that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). Ecclesiastes says the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it — and I find both words kind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the middle of a death sentence, Adam names his wife Eve — 'living' — because she would be the mother of all the living. That is either stubborn hope or real faith, and I think it is faith. He believed the promise of offspring while still wearing the sentence for his sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God does not leave them in their fig leaves. He makes coats of animal skins and clothes them Himself — the first death in the garden, and it is God who does the killing and the clothing. I do not pretend to understand all of it, but I know the shape: covering comes at a cost, and the cost is borne by Another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.' The words sound like an admission and a grief at once. Then the sentence trails off — 'lest he reach out his hand... and live forever' — and that unfinished line is a mercy. Forever in a broken body, forever knowing good and evil without healing, would be no gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So the Lord sends him out of Eden, and the wording is almost gentle: to till the ground from which he was taken. The same work as before, only now outside the garden and against resistance. His vocation is not cancelled; it follows him out the gate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He drove the man out and set cherubim at the east of Eden, with a flaming sword turning every way. Guarded, not simply abandoned — the way back is kept, though not by us. When Moses later wove cherubim into the veil of the tabernacle, I wonder if he remembered this gate and hoped.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
